title: Getting the Latest Row: TOP 1 Needs an Index
description: Finding the latest row with TOP 1 + ORDER BY scans and sorts everything; an index on the sort column reads just the first row.
narrative:
## Scenario
A dashboard shows the single most recent order: `SELECT TOP 1 ... FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderDate DESC`. On a 200,000-row table it is surprisingly slow for a query that returns just **one** row.

## Why it's slow
`Orders` is clustered on `OrderId`, but **nothing** orders the rows by `OrderDate`. To find the latest one, SQL Server must read *every* row (a **Clustered Index Scan**) and then perform a **Top-N Sort** to bring the newest to the top. Returning 1 row costs a full-table scan.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders` reading ~200k rows.
- A **Sort** (Top-N) operator — the giveaway that the engine had to order the data itself.

## The concept
An index is stored **in order**. With an index keyed on `OrderDate`, the newest row is simply the last entry — SQL Server reads the tail of the index and stops. No scan, no sort. This is why an index on the `ORDER BY` column turns a full scan into a couple of reads.
hints: The query returns 1 row but is slow — look at how many rows the plan actually reads.
There is a Sort (Top-N) operator. SQL had to order the whole table because no index provides OrderDate order.
Create an index on the ORDER BY column: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON Orders(OrderDate);
